name: Mountains: How They Rose and Who Climbed Them
description: The slow collisions that raised the Alps, Andes and Himalayas, the volcanoes that built Fuji and Kilimanjaro, and the people who first stood on the summits.

checkpoints.name: Old ranges
checkpoints.note: The Appalachians and the Urals are among the oldest ranges on our list, raised when ancient continents collided and now worn low by hundreds of millions of years of erosion. The Andes began forming as an ocean plate dived beneath South America.

checkpoints.name: Young giants
checkpoints.note: The Rockies, the Alps, the Himalayas and the Tibetan plateau are far younger. The Himalayas and Mount Everest are still rising as India presses into Asia, which also lifted the plateau behind them.

checkpoints.name: Fire mountains
checkpoints.note: Not every mountain is folded rock: Kilimanjaro, Etna, Fuji, Vesuvius and Mount St. Helens are volcanoes, and Mazama's eruption left a lake. Tambora's eruption in 1815 and Krakatoa's in 1883 changed weather and lives far away. Banff and Yosemite became protected places.

checkpoints.name: To the summits
checkpoints.note: Wegener proposed drifting continents in 1912, and plate tectonics later explained mountain building. Climbers, from the French on Annapurna in 1950 to Hillary and Tenzing on Everest in 1953 and an Italian team on K2 in 1954, reached the highest peaks. Tragedies followed, including 1996.
